posts.title: Chasing fog on the north ridge
posts.excerpt: Four mornings of alarms at 4:40 for one ten-minute window of light.
posts.body:
Fog forecasts are honest about one thing only: they are guesses. I drove up to the north ridge four mornings in a row, and three of them gave me a grey wall and a thermos of cold coffee.

On the fourth morning the cloud sat just below the summits. The ridges came out of it one by one, each a little paler than the last, and for about ten minutes the whole valley looked like layered paper.

What made it work

I used a long lens to stack the ridges, and I underexposed by two thirds of a stop so the brightest fog kept its texture. Everything else was patience.

posts.title: The larch, six winters on
posts.excerpt: One tree, the same spot, every winter since 2020.
posts.body:
There is a single larch in the field behind the old quarry road. I photograph it every winter from the same place, and every year it looks a little different: more lean, fewer branches, a new scar from the ice.

Long projects teach you to see small changes. They also teach you that the best picture is often the plainest one: one tree, one horizon, a lot of white.

posts.title: Notes from the coastal flight
posts.excerpt: Forty minutes in a small plane with the door off.
posts.body:
The pilot banked over Saltmere twice so I could get the lagoon square in the frame. With the door off the wind is loud enough that you stop thinking and just shoot.

From the air, tide channels look like drawings. Shoot fast shutter speeds, keep the horizon out, and let the patterns fill the frame.

posts.title: A city after rain
posts.excerpt: Why I go out the minute the rain stops.
posts.body:
Rain doubles every light in a city. The street becomes a mirror, the windows reflect twice, and for half an hour everything glows.

I shoot these wide open with the focus pulled slightly off, so the lights turn into soft circles. Sharpness is overrated after dark.

posts.title: Under the galaxy core
posts.excerpt: Late summer, a clear moor, and twenty-second exposures.
posts.body:
The galaxy core is only well placed for a few weeks each summer here. This year the moor was clear on the last good night.

Twenty seconds at f/2, ISO 3200, and a red head torch so my eyes stayed adjusted. The faint orange on the horizon is the town fourteen miles away.

posts.title: Long exposures at Corran Head
posts.excerpt: Two minutes of shutter turns a restless sea into glass.
posts.body:
Corran Head has a sea stack that sits perfectly against the evening sun in July. A ten-stop filter and a two-minute exposure smooth the water completely.

Settings

f/11, 120 seconds, ISO 100, ten-stop filter. Bring a towel for the tripod legs; the tide comes in faster than you think.

posts.title: Blue is the colour of snow
posts.excerpt: Before sunrise, snow takes the colour of the sky.
posts.body:
People are surprised that my winter pictures are so blue. Before the sun rises, snow reflects the sky, and the sky is blue. I leave it that way.

Correcting it to white makes a technically neutral picture and a much colder feeling. I would rather keep the hour as it was.

posts.title: Printing the Quiet Weather series
posts.excerpt: Fog is the hardest thing to print well.
posts.body:
Fog lives in the brightest five percent of the image, which is exactly where cheap paper fails. I tested four papers before choosing a soft matte cotton rag.

The final prints are 60 by 90 centimetres, each one checked in daylight before it leaves the studio.

posts.title: Violet Crossing and the arcade
posts.excerpt: One neon sign changed the colour of a whole street.
posts.body: The arcade on Fenn Street turns its sign on at dusk, and the whole crossing goes violet. I stood on the same corner for three evenings until a tram passed at the right moment.

posts.title: Low tide light
posts.excerpt: Wet sand is the best reflector on the coast.
posts.body: At low tide the beach becomes a huge mirror for a few minutes after each wave. I time the shutter to the retreating water.

posts.title: Moonlight is just slow sunlight
posts.excerpt: A full moon and an eight-second exposure.
posts.body: Moonlight is reflected sunlight, so a long enough exposure looks almost like day, but quieter. I keep it a little dark so it still feels like night.

posts.title: Why I shoot the same places
posts.body:
Most of my pictures come from six or seven places within two hours of home. Going back teaches me where the light falls in each season and what the weather is about to do.

The lake in this picture is twenty minutes from my door. I have been there more than a hundred times. This is the morning it was perfectly still.

home.title: Quiet weather, salt light, cities after dark.
Hello
home.text:
I photograph the hours most people sleep through: fog before sunrise, the last light on the coast, and towns after rain.

This site is my portfolio and my notebook. The journal has field notes, settings and the stories behind the pictures.

home.title: Iris Calloway
home.text: Returning to the same place is the whole method.

home.title: Commissions and prints
home.text: I take a small number of commissions each year, from book covers to hotel collections. Every print is made and checked in my studio.

home.title: Working on something?
home.text: Tell me about it. I reply within two days.

about.title: About Iris
about.text:
I am a landscape photographer based in Larch Harbour. I started with a borrowed film camera on the coast and never stopped going back to the same places.

My work has appeared in travel magazines, book covers and two solo exhibitions.

about.title: How I work
about.text:
Small kit, long walks, early alarms. I shoot mostly with one body and two lenses, a tripod, and a lot of patience.

I print everything myself on matte cotton paper, so the quiet tones survive from screen to wall.
The north trail, where most of the Quiet Weather series began.
